newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: FEATURE-Sexual segregation dominates life for Saudi women.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sexual segregation dominates life for Saudi women.

text.p: At the Prince Salman Social Centre in Riyadh, Saudi women pump iron in the weight room or go for the burn at aerobics class. With their bright lycra bodies and Reebok shoes, they could be working out anywhere in the world.

But outside the gates of the single-sex gym, the leotards and faces vanish. Covered in long black robes, the women peer out from behind dark veils as they wait for their male drivers to shuttle them home.

In Saudi Arabia, women are forbidden to drive. They must cover their hair in public and wear the long-sleeved black 'abaya' cloak. And whenever women go out they should be accompanied by their 'mahram' -- a close male relative such as their husband, father or adult son.
"The woman has no identity here without a man," said one young Saudi woman who refused to be named. "I can never be happy in Saudi Arabia. I am treated like a child and have no rights."
Others treasure life in the conservative kingdom. They say they feel safe and fear crime and sexual harassment abroad.
Behind the veils, many women work, own property and have sole control over their money according to the Koran, the Islamic holy book which forms the basis of Saudi law.

"The stereotype of Moslem women as uneducated, downtrodden creatures with no rights and no opportunities is a caricature born of ignorance or malevolence," says a handbook on Saudi Arabia published by the Ministry of Information.
SAUDI WOMEN EDUCATED, BUT WORK BARRIERS STILL EXIST
Many women are highly educated in the male-dominated society, and the number of working women is slowly on the rise.

The latest independent statistics show the employment of women nearly doubled between 1986 and 1991 to 83,000, but 72,000 of these were foreigners. Nonetheless, women work in a wide range of fields, including medicine, education and business. Increasing numbers run their own companies and buy shares in Saudi firms.
King Fahd and his government emphasise raising the number of working women, a goal spelled out in the five-year plan to 2000.
But cultural and religious barriers still exist, and many families frown on working women. A woman is generally expected to give full commitment to her family and home.
And many argue that although women find jobs, they quickly hit a glass ceiling which keeps them from top-level positions.
Others say women are just afraid to fight for their rights.
"Many girls are just afraid to go out and to try to be career women," said Salwa Shaker, a producer on Saudi state-run television and radio.

"I choose to live in Saudi Arabia and don't want to live anywhere else," said Shaker, a married mother of six. "I have goals I haven't accomplished yet. Among them is to show Saudi women that they can be most everything they want to be."
SEXUAL SEGREGATION PERMEATES SOCIAL FABRIC
Despite their active social role, women are rarely seen. With some exceptions, women cannot work where they are exposed to men and are generally sidelined to a women-only workplace.

Many Saudi women are deeply religious and say sexual discrimination contradicts Islam. They say the Koran, which was revealed to Prophet Mohammad 1,400 years ago, gave women rights, including control of wealth and access to education. Many of the current practices are not based on religion, they say.
Sexual segregation permeates the social fabric, from universities and banks to restaurants and social venues such as the Prince Salman centre.
"Universities are separated according to sex," one Saudi woman said. "Girls get to watch male teachers on television screens live and they can call in questions."

Most banks have special women's branches with all-female staff and customers. Restaurants are either for men only or offer an additional 'family section'. A common sign at Riyadh restaurants reads: 'no single women', even in family sections.
Inside, groups are separated from each other by booths with long curtains or wood partitions.
"The way I'm always stuck in a special room makes me feel like I have some contagious disease," one woman said.
Many Saudi women are eager to share stories of incidents they describe as humiliating and demeaning.

"I was in a cafe with two women friends," one woman said. "Four mutawaeen (religious police) stormed in and yelled 'cover your faces', 'where are your mahrams?' and ordered us to leave. My father had to come and pretend we were all his daughters. If he hadn't, I would have hidden in the bathroom overnight."
WOMEN TRY TO FIND WAYS AROUND TABOOS

Women widely disapprove of the driving ban, and many were thrilled when about 50 women, some from prominent families, defied the ban in November 1990 by driving through Riyadh. But cheers gave way to quiet grumbling when the women were briefly detained and reports spread that several had lost their jobs.
Dating is also taboo, but young Saudis have found a way.
"Young women will dress up with a nice black headscarf and cruise down the streets with the chauffeur," a women explained.

"Then two cars pull up next to each other. He or she throws a piece of paper across with a mobile phone number and a false name so they can flirt or chat on the phone," she said. "This seems to be the only way they can get to know each other."

Saudis say many marriages are still arranged, or couples are coaxed into a relationship by their families. Islamic law in force in the kingdom allows for a man to have up to four wives, but polygamy has become very uncommon.
"In the West, men have mistresses. Here they marry both women and it's all on the table," one foreign resident said.
Writer Intisaar al-Ageel says Saudi Arabia is changing gradually and cannot rush into reforms on women's rights.

"What can the government do but keep a wise balance?" she said. "Some people are scared of new steps and change. The government always has to keep a thermometer of public opinion. If the public isn't ready, you can't force them."
